concept.name: Sample mean
concept.definition: The arithmetic average of the observations in a sample, denoted x-bar. It is the standard estimator of the population mean and is unbiased: its expected value equals the population mean.
concept.intuition: It is your best single-number guess of the true average when you can only see a slice of the data - the mean of the 250 daily returns you observed standing in for the mean of the return-generating process.
concept.mechanics: Sum the sample values and divide by the sample size n. Its own sampling distribution has mean mu and standard deviation sigma/sqrt(n) (the standard error), becoming approximately normal for large n by the central limit theorem.
concept.formula: x_bar = (1/n) * SUM_{i=1..n} x_i, where x_i are the sample observations and n is the sample size; E[x_bar] = mu and Var(x_bar) = sigma^2/n for i.i.d. samples.
concept.failure_modes: As an estimator it inherits the arithmetic mean's fragility: a handful of extreme observations (a crash day) can dominate it, and for heavy-tailed distributions without a finite mean (Cauchy) collecting more data never improves it. Serial correlation in returns inflates its true standard error beyond sigma/sqrt(n).
concept.misconceptions: The sample mean is a random variable, not the population mean - it differs from mu on every sample, and quoting it without a standard error hides that uncertainty. 'Unbiased' also does not mean 'accurate for your sample'; it is a statement about averaging over many hypothetical samples.
concept.example: For n = 20 daily returns summing to 2.1%, the sample mean is 0.105% per day; with sigma = 1.5%, its standard error is 0.34%, so the estimate is statistically indistinguishable from zero.
